cert.udemy_subtitle: 4 Full-Length 65-Question Mocks (260 Scenarios) · Serverless, Q Developer, Bedrock Guardrails & Testing

questions.stem: A financial services engineering team maintains 42 legacy Java 8 Maven microservices running on Amazon ECS and must upgrade them to Java 17 before an upcoming compliance audit. Senior developers want an AI-assisted workflow inside their IDE that automatically analyzes dependency trees, updates deprecated Jakarta EE APIs, compiles the project, and produces a reviewable diff so engineers can verify business logic before merging. Which AWS capability best meets this requirement?
options: Enable Amazon CodeGuru Profiler on the running ECS tasks to automatically rewrite Java 8 bytecode into Java 17 compatible JAR archives during live traffic.

Use Amazon Q Developer Agent for code transformation to automate the Java 8 to Java 17 migration, generate build-verified code diffs, and let developers review and approve the changes before committing.
Export the Maven repositories to Amazon S3 and invoke Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel on each .java file independently without resolving pom.xml transitive dependencies.
Configure AWS Elastic Beanstalk managed platform updates to upgrade the JVM runtime and rewrite deprecated javax package imports inside the compiled WAR files automatically.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because Amazon Q Developer Agent for code transformation specifically automates Java 8/11 to Java 17/21 upgrades by inspecting the project structure, upgrading pom.xml dependencies, refactoring deprecated APIs, running Maven builds in a sandbox, and presenting a clear diff for human developer supervision prior to merge. Option A is wrong because CodeGuru Profiler analyzes runtime CPU and latency hotspots and never rewrites source code or upgrades language versions. Option C is wrong because sending isolated source files to a foundation model ignores multi-file dependency resolution and Maven compilation verification. Option D is wrong because Elastic Beanstalk platform updates change host runtimes but never refactor application source code or package imports.
questions.use_case: Enterprise platform teams use Amazon Q Developer code transformation to compress multi-quarter Java 8/11 modernization backlogs into days while keeping developers in control of pull request approvals and integration testing.
questions.hack: Automated Java 8/11 to 17/21 upgrades with dependency resolution and reviewable diffs = Amazon Q Developer Agent for code transformation.

questions.stem: During a pull request review for a new AWS Lambda support triage API generated with an AI coding assistant, a lead developer discovers two issues: the handler interpolates raw customer ticket text directly into a system prompt sent to Amazon Bedrock without input filtering, and it falls back to a hardcoded third-party CRM API key string when an environment variable is absent. Which remediation plan addresses both risks according to AWS security best practices?
options: Base64-encode the fallback CRM API key inside the Python module and strip HTML tags from the customer ticket text using a regular expression before calling Bedrock.

Remove the hardcoded fallback key, retrieve the CRM secret at runtime from AWS Secrets Manager using the Lambda execution role, separate system instructions from untrusted user content in the Bedrock Converse API, and attach Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with prompt attack filtering.
Move the hardcoded CRM API key into the SAM template.yaml Parameters section with NoEcho enabled and increase the Bedrock model temperature to 0.9 to make prompt injection outputs less deterministic.
Store the CRM API key in a public Amazon S3 bucket protected by an obscure object prefix and route all Bedrock calls through an AWS WAF rate-based rule.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because it eliminates hardcoded credentials by fetching secrets dynamically from AWS Secrets Manager via least-privilege IAM, cleanly isolates system instructions from untrusted user messages in the Converse API, and enforces Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to detect and block prompt injection attacks. Option A is wrong because Base64 is reversible encoding rather than secret management, and HTML regex stripping does not stop natural-language prompt injection. Option C is wrong because NoEcho only masks CloudFormation console output rather than rotating or protecting secrets at runtime, and higher temperature worsens output unpredictability without mitigating prompt attacks. Option D is wrong because security by obscurity in a public S3 bucket violates least privilege and AWS WAF inspects HTTP traffic rather than semantic LLM prompt attacks.
questions.use_case: Security-conscious serverless teams combine AI code security reviews, AWS Secrets Manager runtime retrieval, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to harden AI-authored GenAI endpoints before production launch.
questions.hack: Hardcoded fallback secret + prompt injection in AI-generated Lambda = Secrets Manager + separate Converse roles + Bedrock Guardrails prompt attack filter.

questions.stem: A Python developer owns an AWS Lambda pricing engine that queries Amazon DynamoDB and publishes discount events to Amazon EventBridge. Unit test coverage sits at 34%, and many tax boundary conditions are untested. The developer wants to use AI-assisted test generation to rapidly create pytest unit tests that validate edge cases inside AWS CodeBuild without requiring live AWS credentials or incurring DynamoDB charges. What should the developer do?
options: Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the Lambda function so X-Ray automatically generates and runs unit test suites whenever a new version is published.
Configure AWS CodeBuild to provision a dedicated DynamoDB table and EventBridge bus on every git commit and invoke the live Lambda function in production with synthetic test payloads.

Use Amazon Q Developer test generation to author pytest unit tests covering the uncovered branches, and mock Boto3 DynamoDB and EventBridge calls with botocore.stub.Stubber or moto so the suite executes offline in CodeBuild.
Use Amazon Q Developer to disable conditional tax branches and rely solely on Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics Canaries after production deployment to catch pricing calculation bugs.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because Amazon Q Developer can analyze function logic and generate targeted pytest unit tests for uncovered boundary conditions, while mocking AWS SDK calls with botocore Stubber or moto keeps unit tests fast, deterministic, credential-free, and cost-free inside CodeBuild. Option B is wrong because provisioning real cloud resources on every unit test run is slow and costly, and invoking production with synthetic payloads risks corrupting live data. Option A is wrong because AWS X-Ray traces live distributed requests and never generates unit tests. Option D is wrong because deleting business logic and relying exclusively on post-deploy canaries lets critical pricing defects reach customers.
questions.use_case: Serverless engineering teams pair Amazon Q Developer unit test generation with botocore Stubber or moto in CodeBuild to raise branch coverage above 80% with sub-second offline test execution.
questions.hack: AI-assisted offline unit tests for Boto3 Lambdas in CodeBuild = Amazon Q Developer test generation + botocore Stubber or moto mocks.

questions.stem: An e-commerce API backed by 14 AWS Lambda microservices experiences sporadic HTTP 504 timeouts during flash sales. On-call developers struggle to write complex regex queries across all 14 log groups to correlate requestId values, cold start init durations from REPORT lines, and downstream latency spikes. Which approach enables the fastest unified root-cause investigation?
options: Download each Lambda log stream manually from the AWS Management Console as CSV files and search them sequentially on a local laptop using grep.
Switch all 14 Lambda functions from standard JSON logging to unstructured plain-text print statements so CloudWatch Metrics can automatically graph requestId timeouts.
Export every CloudWatch Log group to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive every hour and inspect the archives with Amazon S3 Select.

Select all 14 Lambda log groups in Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights and use natural-language query generation (or Amazon Q Developer operational investigation) to build a multi-log-group query correlating requestId, Init Duration, and timeout entries.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because CloudWatch Logs Insights natively queries up to dozens of log groups simultaneously and supports natural-language query generation (alongside Amazon Q Developer investigations) to rapidly synthesize fields, filter, parse, and stats queries that correlate requestId values, Init Duration spikes, and timeout errors. Option A is wrong because manual downloads and local grep do not scale during an active incident. Option C is wrong because S3 Glacier Deep Archive has hours-long retrieval times and cannot be queried interactively for live incident triage. Option B is wrong because unstructured print statements degrade queryability compared to structured JSON logs and CloudWatch Metrics does not automatically graph arbitrary requestId strings.
questions.use_case: SRE and backend teams query correlated serverless microservices in seconds using CloudWatch Logs Insights natural-language query generation across multiple Lambda log groups.
questions.hack: Correlate requestId and Init Duration across many Lambda log groups quickly = CloudWatch Logs Insights multi-log-group query with natural-language generation.

questions.stem: A SaaS analytics startup is building a Python FastAPI service on AWS Fargate that integrates with Amazon Bedrock to stream answers to browser clients in real time and invoke internal SQL lookup tools. Product managers want the flexibility to switch between Anthropic Claude and Amazon Nova models by changing only a modelId configuration value, without rewriting request body schemas or parsing logic. Which Boto3 Bedrock Runtime pattern should the developer implement?
options: Call bedrock-runtime invoke_model with model-specific JSON payload templates for each provider and buffer the entire completion in memory before returning HTTP 200.

Call bedrock-runtime converse_stream with a standardized messages array and toolConfig definition so streaming token deltas and tool-use blocks follow one uniform schema across supported foundation models.
Invoke bedrock-agent start_ingestion_job on every user chat turn so Bedrock transforms model responses into uniform CSV chunks.
Use Amazon API Gateway VTL mapping templates to translate Anthropic JSON schemas into Amazon Nova schemas inside a REST API proxy without modifying the Fargate code.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because the Amazon Bedrock Converse API (specifically converse_stream for streaming) provides a single, consistent request and response schema across supported foundation models, including multi-turn messages, system prompts, guardrails, and toolConfig function calling, letting developers swap modelId without code rewrites. Option A is wrong because invoke_model requires provider-specific payload formats and buffering defeats real-time token streaming. Option C is wrong because start_ingestion_job indexes documents into a Knowledge Base rather than executing real-time streaming chat completions. Option D is wrong because VTL mapping templates in API Gateway cannot handle bi-directional streaming event streams cleanly and add brittle translation logic that Converse eliminates natively.
questions.use_case: Multi-model GenAI backends standardize on Bedrock converse and converse_stream so product teams can A/B test or upgrade foundation models via a single modelId environment variable.
questions.hack: One uniform API for streaming + tool use across multiple Bedrock models = bedrock-runtime converse_stream.

questions.stem: A developer uses an AI coding assistant to prototype a Python AWS Lambda data parser. The assistant suggests installing an obscure package named py-aws-json-fast-utils in requirements.txt. A security engineer warns that attackers register package names frequently hallucinated by LLMs on public PyPI (slopsquatting) to execute malicious code during CI/CD builds. Which control best prevents hallucinated or unapproved third-party dependencies from entering production builds?
options: Configure AWS CodeBuild to run pip install with the --trusted-host flag so TLS certificate errors never block third-party package downloads.
Move all pip install commands out of CodeBuild and execute them directly inside the Lambda handler at runtime using subprocess so packages never reside in the deployment ZIP.

Host an internal AWS CodeArtifact repository with curated allowlisted package approval policies, enforce hash-pinned lockfiles in requirements.txt, and run automated dependency vulnerability scanning during CodeBuild.
Grant the CodeBuild service role AdministratorAccess so pip can query IAM Access Analyzer before downloading wheels from public PyPI.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because AWS CodeArtifact acts as a controlled private package proxy where organizations approve vetted packages and block arbitrary unapproved PyPI downloads, while hash-pinned lockfiles and automated vulnerability scanning in CodeBuild stop hallucinated or tampered dependencies from entering artifacts. Option A is wrong because --trusted-host weakens TLS verification and does nothing to block malicious packages. Option B is wrong because running pip install at Lambda runtime slows cold starts, requires public internet access, and still executes malicious package setup scripts inside production. Option D is wrong because IAM Access Analyzer evaluates IAM permissions rather than Python package provenance, and granting AdministratorAccess violates least privilege.
questions.use_case: DevSecOps pipelines pair AWS CodeArtifact curated repositories with hash-locked requirements and Amazon Inspector / SCA scans to eliminate slopsquatting and supply-chain attacks in AI-assisted coding workflows.
questions.hack: Block hallucinated AI-suggested packages (slopsquatting) in CI/CD = AWS CodeArtifact curated repo + hash-pinned lockfile + automated dependency scanning.

questions.stem: An order-ingestion Lambda function writes JSON events to a provisioned Amazon DynamoDB table configured with 2,000 Write Capacity Units (WCUs). During peak hours, developers observe frequent Boto3 ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors even though Amazon CloudWatch reports that table-level ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits never exceeds 450 WCUs. Inspecting the table schema reveals that the partition key is order_status, and 92% of new writes carry the value PENDING. How should the developer resolve the throttling?
options: Increase the DynamoDB table provisioned capacity from 2,000 WCUs to 10,000 WCUs while keeping order_status as the sole partition key.
Enable DynamoDB Streams with NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES so DynamoDB automatically splits the single PENDING partition key across multiple Regions.
Deploy Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the table because DAX absorbs unlimited concurrent writes to a single hot partition key.
Redesign the partition key to a high-cardinality attribute such as order_id (or apply write sharding such as PENDING#0 through PENDING#19) so writes distribute evenly across physical partitions.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because each individual DynamoDB physical partition is capped at 1,000 WCUs regardless of total table capacity; sending 92% of writes to a single low-cardinality partition key (order_status=PENDING) causes hot-partition throttling. Switching to a high-cardinality partition key like order_id or adding a random/calculated shard suffix spreads write traffic across many physical partitions. Option A is wrong because scaling table capacity cannot overcome the hard 1,000 WCU per-partition ceiling on one single key value. Option C is wrong because DAX is a write-through read cache and still forwards every write synchronously to the underlying DynamoDB hot partition. Option B is wrong because DynamoDB Streams records item changes for consumers and does not re-partition or scale write throughput.
questions.use_case: High-throughput event ingestion platforms avoid single-key hot partitions by using UUID/order_id partition keys and using write-sharded GSIs when querying active status buckets.
questions.hack: ProvisionedThroughputExceededException when table Consumed WCU is low + low-cardinality PK (e.g., status=PENDING) = hot partition -> use high-cardinality PK or write sharding.

questions.stem: A medical device manufacturer hosts 8,000 PDF maintenance manuals in an Amazon S3 bucket that is updated nightly. Field technicians need an internal Q&A web application that answers repair questions grounded strictly in the latest manuals, filters results by device_model metadata, and cites source documents without retraining or fine-tuning a foundation model. Which Amazon Bedrock architecture requires the least custom infrastructure code?
options: Launch a Bedrock Custom Model fine-tuning job every night using the PDF files stored in Amazon S3 so the model weights memorize updated manuals.

Create an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base backed by the S3 data source with metadata JSON sidecar files, trigger StartIngestionJob when manuals update, and query it using the Bedrock Agent Runtime RetrieveAndGenerate API with a metadata filter.
Download all 8,000 PDF files into AWS Lambda /tmp storage during every user request and concatenate their text into the Bedrock Converse prompt.
Store the PDFs in Amazon DynamoDB items and execute a DynamoDB Scan with a FilterExpression for each technician question before calling Amazon Comprehend.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases natively implements managed Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): it chunks, embeds, and indexes S3 PDFs with metadata sidecars on StartIngestionJob, and RetrieveAndGenerate filters by device_model, retrieves relevant chunks, generates grounded answers, and returns inline citations without fine-tuning. Option A is wrong because fine-tuning is slow, expensive, unsuitable for nightly factual knowledge updates, and does not produce source citations. Option C is wrong because 8,000 PDFs exceed both Lambda /tmp limits and foundation model context windows. Option D is wrong because DynamoDB has a 400 KB item limit, Scan is inefficient, and Amazon Comprehend extracts entities rather than generating grounded conversational answers.
questions.use_case: Internal enterprise portals use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with S3 metadata filtering and RetrieveAndGenerate to deliver fresh, cited RAG answers with minimal glue code.
questions.hack: Grounded Q&A over frequently updated S3 PDFs + metadata filter + citations + no fine-tuning = Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases + RetrieveAndGenerate.

questions.stem: A backend engineer is developing a serverless inventory API defined in an AWS SAM template.yaml file with three Python AWS Lambda functions backed by Amazon DynamoDB. Before pushing code to Git, the engineer wants to execute end-to-end HTTP requests locally on their workstation against both the API Gateway routes and a local DynamoDB instance without deploying any resources to AWS. Which local testing workflow should the engineer use?
options: Run sam deploy --no-execute-changeset to execute Lambda functions inside local Docker containers without touching an AWS account.
Run aws cloudformation validate-template because template validation spins up an emulated API Gateway and DynamoDB process on localhost.

Run sam local start-api attached via --docker-network to a local DynamoDB Local container, override the Boto3 DynamoDB endpoint_url via a local environment JSON file, and send HTTP test requests to http://127.0.0.1:3000.
Run aws dynamodb scan --local-only from the AWS CLI because the AWS CLI bundles an embedded API Gateway proxy.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because AWS SAM CLI's sam local start-api emulates API Gateway and executes Lambda handlers locally in Docker containers; attaching it to the same --docker-network as a DynamoDB Local container and pointing Boto3 endpoint_url via --env-vars enables full offline local integration testing. Option B is wrong because validate-template checks only CloudFormation syntax and never runs application code. Option A is wrong because sam deploy --no-execute-changeset uploads artifacts to S3 and creates a CloudFormation Change Set in AWS rather than running locally. Option D is wrong because there is no --local-only embedded API Gateway proxy in the AWS CLI.
questions.use_case: Serverless developers run sam local start-api alongside DynamoDB Local on a shared Docker network to iterate on API contracts and queries offline before pushing branches.
questions.hack: Test SAM API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB locally offline = sam local start-api + --docker-network + DynamoDB Local + endpoint_url override.

questions.stem: A wealth management application calls multiple Amazon Bedrock foundation models to summarize client portfolios and draft advisor emails. Compliance mandates that Social Security numbers and credit card numbers must be masked or blocked in BOTH user prompts and model outputs, and any prompt asking for unapproved cryptocurrency tax evasion advice must be denied consistently across every model without rewriting individual system prompts. What is the most maintainable solution?
options: Configure AWS Shield Advanced on the Application Load Balancer to inspect JSON response payloads for credit card numbers and denied topics.
Append a 300-word compliance disclaimer to the bottom of every model's system prompt and trust the LLM to never emit PII.
Enable Amazon Macie on the AWS Lambda execution logs so Macie retroactively blocks HTTP responses after they reach the customer's browser.

Configure an Amazon Bedrock Guardrail with Sensitive Information filters (PII redaction/blocking) and Denied Topics policies, publish a versioned guardrail, and pass guardrailIdentifier and guardrailVersion on every Bedrock Converse or InvokeModel call.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides centralized, model-agnostic safeguards that inspect both incoming prompts and outgoing model responses for PII (block or mask), denied topics, harmful content, and prompt attacks via a single versioned guardrailIdentifier passed to Converse or InvokeModel. Option B is wrong because prompt-only instructions can be bypassed by jailbreaks and require duplicating rules across every prompt template. Option C is wrong because Amazon Macie scans Amazon S3 objects asynchronously and cannot intercept or block live Bedrock API responses. Option A is wrong because AWS Shield Advanced mitigates DDoS attacks rather than semantic LLM policy violations or PII redaction.
questions.use_case: Regulated fintech and healthcare platforms enforce uniform PII redaction and denied-topic compliance across all GenAI apps via versioned Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.
questions.hack: Centrally block/mask PII and denied topics in both LLM inputs and outputs across models = Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (guardrailIdentifier + guardrailVersion).

questions.stem: A global customer-support platform invokes Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock in us-east-1 from Python Lambda functions. During peak North American business hours, sudden traffic spikes trigger Boto3 ThrottlingException errors even though average hourly token volume does not justify buying expensive 24/7 Provisioned Throughput commitments. Which combination of changes best improves resilience and burst capacity at minimal cost?
options: Disable retries in Boto3 Config so failed requests return immediately, and hardcode a 60-second time.sleep call before every Bedrock API invocation.

Switch the modelId to an Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region Inference Profile (such as a US system-defined inference profile) to dynamically route bursts across multiple US Regions, and configure Boto3 Config with adaptive retry mode and exponential backoff with jitter.
Purchase dedicated Provisioned Throughput model units across four AWS Regions simultaneously and route every request through Amazon SQS FIFO with a 15-minute delay.
Increase the Lambda function memory to 10,240 MB because Bedrock account token-per-minute quotas scale automatically with Lambda RAM.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region Inference Profiles automatically distribute on-demand inference requests across multiple AWS Regions within a geography at no extra per-token cost, dramatically increasing burst throughput, while Boto3 adaptive retry mode handles residual transient throttling cleanly via exponential backoff with jitter. Option A is wrong because disabling retries leaves callers exposed to transient spikes and sleeping 60 seconds degrades user latency and wastes Lambda duration billing. Option C is wrong because Provisioned Throughput across four Regions violates the minimal-cost requirement for spiky traffic. Option D is wrong because Lambda memory scales Lambda vCPU/network, not Amazon Bedrock service-side token quotas.
questions.use_case: Production GenAI applications adopt Bedrock Cross-Region Inference Profiles plus Boto3 adaptive retries to absorb bursty on-demand traffic without paying for idle Provisioned Throughput.
questions.hack: Bedrock ThrottlingException on spiky traffic without paying for 24/7 Provisioned Throughput = Cross-Region Inference Profile + Boto3 adaptive retries.

questions.stem: A developer instruments a Python AWS Lambda order-processing function with the AWS X-Ray SDK so operations engineers can search traces by customer_tier = 'enterprise' in the X-Ray console and ServiceLens Analytics. After deployment, traces appear normally in the console, yet filter expressions like annotation.customer_tier = "enterprise" return zero results even though customer_tier is visible inside the raw trace JSON document under the subsegment. What caused this issue?
options: AWS X-Ray only allows filtering on numeric values and ignores string attributes on Python runtimes.
The Lambda execution role is missing the xray:IndexMetadata IAM permission required to search trace attributes.
The developer attached customer_tier using put_metadata() instead of put_annotation(), and X-Ray only indexes annotations for filter expressions.
The X-Ray sampling rule must be set to 100% before any filter expression can match attributes in the X-Ray console.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because AWS X-Ray distinguishes strictly between annotations and metadata: annotations (put_annotation) are key-value pairs of strings, numbers, or booleans that X-Ray indexes for use in filter expressions, whereas metadata (put_metadata) stores arbitrary unindexed JSON objects visible only when inspecting an individual trace. Option B is wrong because no xray:IndexMetadata IAM action exists. Option A is wrong because X-Ray annotations support strings, numbers, and booleans across all runtimes. Option D is wrong because sampling rate controls what fraction of requests are traced, not whether existing traces have indexed annotations.
questions.use_case: Microservice teams tag traces with put_annotation for high-value business dimensions like tenant_id or customer_tier so on-call engineers can slice P99 latency per tier in X-Ray Analytics.
questions.hack: X-Ray filter expression finds 0 traces even though field is inside trace JSON = used put_metadata (unindexed) instead of put_annotation (indexed).

questions.stem: A serverless payments team deploys an AWS Lambda function using AWS SAM and wants every production release to shift 10% of live traffic to the new Lambda version for 5 minutes before shifting the remaining 90%. Before any customer traffic reaches the new version, a validation Lambda must execute smoke tests against the new version and signal AWS CodeDeploy, and any spike in Lambda errors must automatically roll back the alias. Which SAM template configuration achieves this?
options: Enable AutoPublishAlias: $LATEST and configure Amazon EventBridge to run a cron rule that updates the alias weight manually every 5 minutes.
Set ReservedConcurrentExecutions: 10 and attach an AWS Step Functions Wait state of 300 seconds inside the SAM Globals block.
Configure DeploymentPreference with Type: AllAtOnce and specify Hooks.PostTraffic to block initial traffic until smoke tests pass.

Set AutoPublishAlias: live, DeploymentPreference with Type: Canary10Percent5Minutes, Hooks.PreTraffic pointing to the validation Lambda (which calls codedeploy:PutLifecycleEventHookExecutionStatus), and Alarms referencing a CloudWatch error alarm.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because AWS SAM integrates directly with AWS CodeDeploy via AutoPublishAlias and DeploymentPreference: Canary10Percent5Minutes shifts 10% for 5 minutes then 100%, Hooks.PreTraffic runs before any live traffic shifts and reports Succeeded or Failed via codedeploy:PutLifecycleEventHookExecutionStatus, and Alarms triggers automatic rollback on breach. Option B is wrong because ReservedConcurrentExecutions caps concurrency rather than performing canary traffic shifting. Option C is wrong because AllAtOnce shifts 100% immediately and PostTraffic runs after traffic has already shifted. Option A is wrong because $LATEST is mutable and cannot be used as a CodeDeploy alias target for weighted traffic shifting.
questions.use_case: Fintech API teams enforce safe serverless releases using SAM Canary10Percent5Minutes with PreTraffic contract checks and CloudWatch error alarms for zero-touch rollbacks.
questions.hack: SAM 10% for 5 min + pre-traffic smoke test + auto-rollback = AutoPublishAlias + DeploymentPreference Canary10Percent5Minutes + PreTraffic hook + Alarms.

questions.stem: A security audit flags an AWS Lambda execution role powering an Amazon Bedrock document summarizer because it uses the managed policy AmazonBedrockFullAccess (bedrock:* on Resource: *). The Lambda function only calls ConverseStream using a specific US Anthropic Claude inference profile and applies one specific Bedrock Guardrail version. How should the developer rewrite the IAM execution role policy to adhere strictly to least privilege?
options: Replace AmazonBedrockFullAccess with a custom inline or managed policy granting only bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream on the specific inference profile and underlying regional foundation model ARNs, plus bedrock:ApplyGuardrail scoped to the exact guardrail ARN.
Keep bedrock:* on Resource: * but attach an AWS Organizations Service Control Policy denying bedrock:DeleteGuardrail for the entire account.
Remove all Bedrock permissions from the Lambda execution role and pass an IAM user's static AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID via Lambda environment variables instead.
Grant bedrock:InvokeModel* on Resource: * and rely solely on VPC Security Groups to restrict which foundation models the Lambda can call.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because least-privilege IAM for Bedrock limits actions to the exact runtime operations needed (bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream and bedrock:ApplyGuardrail) and scopes Resource ARNs to the specific inference profile, its underlying foundation models, and the specific guardrail rather than wildcarding bedrock:*. Option B is wrong because retaining bedrock:* still allows creating fine-tuning jobs, invoking expensive unapproved models, or modifying agents. Option C is wrong because static IAM user keys in Lambda environment variables violate credential hygiene and still require scoped policies. Option D is wrong because Security Groups operate at TCP/IP layer 4 and cannot distinguish between different Bedrock models or API actions.
questions.use_case: Cloud security teams enforce model allowlists and cost controls by scoping Lambda execution roles to exact Bedrock inference profile, foundation model, and guardrail ARNs.
questions.hack: Least-privilege IAM for Bedrock streaming + Guardrail = scope bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream and bedrock:ApplyGuardrail to exact model/profile/guardrail ARNs.

questions.stem: A developer builds a Python 3.12 AWS Lambda microservice that imports heavy validation and data-mapping libraries, causing cold starts of 2.8 seconds on API Gateway requests. Traffic is bursty and intermittent throughout the day, so paying continuously for Provisioned Concurrency across dozens of environments is too expensive. The developer wants to reduce cold start latency by up to 10x with minimal ongoing idle cost while ensuring unique cryptographic nonces are never duplicated across restored microVMs. What should the developer do?
options: Move all library import statements inside the lambda_handler function body so Python defers loading modules until after the cold start completes.
Set Lambda Provisioned Concurrency to 50 on the $LATEST qualifier so AWS freezes memory snapshots before every API request.

Enable AWS Lambda SnapStart on published versions of the Python function, point the API Gateway integration at a versioned alias, and register an after_restore runtime hook to refresh random seeds and re-establish ephemeral network connections.
Decrease the Lambda memory allocation from 1,024 MB to 128 MB so the Firecracker microVM allocates fewer memory pages during initialization.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because AWS Lambda SnapStart (supported for Java, Python, and .NET) initializes the function once upon version publication, snapshots the initialized Firecracker microVM memory and disk state, and resumes from the encrypted cache on cold starts, slashing latency without 24/7 Provisioned Concurrency costs; after_restore runtime hooks handle uniqueness (RNG seeds, fresh DB/TLS sessions) cleanly. Option B is wrong because Provisioned Concurrency incurs continuous hourly charges and cannot be configured on $LATEST. Option A is wrong because moving imports inside the handler makes initialization run on every invocation rather than during SnapStart checkpointing. Option D is wrong because reducing memory reduces CPU proportionally, making cold starts even slower.
questions.use_case: Python, Java, and .NET serverless API teams enable Lambda SnapStart on published aliases with restore hooks to deliver sub-second cold starts without paying for idle Provisioned Concurrency.
questions.hack: Fast cold starts for Java/Python/.NET without 24/7 Provisioned Concurrency cost + fresh uniqueness = Lambda SnapStart on published version/alias + after_restore hook.
